newsitem.title: BAHRAIN: Gulf team awaits Bahrain response on row with Qatar.
newsitem.headline: Gulf team awaits Bahrain response on row with Qatar.

text.p: Four Gulf Arab foreign ministers concluded talks in Manama on Monday as part of efforts to ease tensions between Bahrain and Qatar fueled by a border row.
The foreign ministers of Saudi Arabia, Kuwait, Oman and the United Arab Emirates met as a committee with Bahrain's Emir Sheikh Isa bin Sulman al-Khalifa and other officials.
They said they were waiting for Manama's response to their proposals for improved ties with Doha.
Saudi Foreign Minister Prince Saud al-Faisal said the committee "provided formulas that will maintain the interests of both countries and restore their ties". He gave no further details.

Qatar's Foreign Minister Sheikh Hamad bin Jassim bin Jabr al-Thani told the official Qatar News Agency after separate talks with the team in Doha late on Sunday that he expected both countries to sign an agreement to boost bilateral ties in Saudi Arabia later this week.
"The committee is waiting for Bahrain's response to its recommendations," the Saudi foreign minister told Bahrain's official Gulf News Agency.
"If we get the approval, we will go ahead with the signing of the agreement between the two countries," he said before leaving Bahrain.
"Qatar and Bahrain will sign in Jeddah at the week's end the text of the agreement to bolster ties," Sheikh Hamad said on Sunday. "The text will not affect the 1990 agreement".
He was referring to an accord that envisaged settlement of the dispute by the International Court of Justice in The Hague. Manama has opposed the move and insists on a regional solution.

The committee, set up by a Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC) summit in December, failed to convince the two countries to agree to a memorandum of understanding during two meetings in Riyadh earlier this month, Gulf Arab officials said.
Qatar and Bahrain are locked in a long-standing dispute over small islands, sandbanks and reefs in the Gulf, controlled by Manama since the 1930s, but also claimed by Doha.
Ties were further strained after Bahrain accused two Qataris of spying -- which Doha denied -- and boycotted the GCC summit in Qatar. Bahrain later pardoned the two Qataris.
